title: Context window filling up
summary: Each turn adds tokens to the conversation. See when it no longer fits, and what you must drop or summarise.

verdicts.text: The conversation no longer fits. Something gets cut, and often the oldest part, which may hold the instructions or facts you still need. Summarise or retrieve instead of replaying everything.
Close to the limit. Long inputs or tool results could push it over on the next turn.
Plenty of room.

tries: Shrink tokens per turn by trimming tool output.

title: Temperature and top-p
summary: The model scores candidate next tokens. Temperature reshapes those scores, and top-p drops the unlikely tail. See how the odds change.

readouts.label: Chance of the most likely token
Chance of anything but the top token

verdicts.text: At a high temperature unlikely tokens get real probability. Output varies more and is more likely to wander.
The top token is almost certain, so the answers are nearly deterministic.
A balanced spread.

tries: Lower top-p to cut the tail.

title: Cost and prompt caching
summary: Input tokens, output tokens and cached prefixes decide the bill and the wait. Enter your own prices, since they change.

inputs.label: Share of the input that is a cached prefix
Price of cached input compared with normal

vars: reqs * inp * (1 - cached/100) / 1000000 * pin + reqs * inp * cached/100 / 1000000 * pin * disc/100

verdicts.text: Input dominates. A long, stable prefix like instructions and tool definitions is the best candidate for caching.
Output dominates. Shorter answers or a smaller model will help more than caching.
Input and output costs are balanced.

tries: Cache 80 percent of a long prompt.
Raise output length until output costs dominate.

chart.y: reqs * inp * (1 - cached/100) / 1000000 * pin + reqs * inp * cached/100 / 1000000 * pin * disc/100 + reqs * out / 1000000 * pout
chart.title: Daily cost against caching

title: How many eval cases you need
summary: Two models score differently on your tests. See whether the gap is real or just noise from a small test set.
vars: sqrt(pa * (1 - pa) / n + pb * (1 - pb) / n)

verdicts.text: The gap is inside the noise. You cannot say one model is better from this test set. Add cases, or test on harder ones.
The gap is larger than the sampling noise, so it is probably real. It may still not be the gap that matters for your users.

tries: Use 200 cases with a 4 point gap.

title: Tool loop token growth
summary: Each tool call adds its result to the context, and the whole context is sent again at every step. See how input tokens add up.

inputs.label: Share of repeated input served from cache

readouts.label: Input tokens processed over the loop
Context size at the last step

verdicts.text: Total input grows with the square of the number of steps. Trim tool results, summarise as you go, or cache the prefix.
The context is getting big, which costs money and can bury what matters.
A short loop with compact results.

chart.title: Input grows faster than the number of steps

title: Tool arguments and schemas
summary: A model fills in the arguments for a tool. See how the chance that every field is valid falls as fields are added, and how tight schemas and retries help.

inputs.label: Retries with the validation error shown
Schema uses enums and clear descriptions

verdicts.text: Even with retries, one call in ten ends in an error. Reduce the number of arguments, use enums and defaults, and return clear validation messages.
Retries save you here, but each costs time and tokens. A tighter schema helps more.
Most calls are valid on the first try.

tries: Use 15 arguments with no strict schema.

title: The three risky capabilities
summary: An agent is most dangerous when it combines private data, untrusted content and a way to send data out. Switch them on to see the risk.

inputs.label: The agent can read private data
The agent reads content you do not control (web, email, tickets)
The agent can send data out (email, HTTP, a link it renders)
A person approves each outbound action

nodes.label: Agent
nodes.sub: all3 ? "all three present" : n + " of 3 present"

verdicts.text: Hidden instructions in the content can tell the agent to read private data and send it out, and nothing stops it. Remove one of the three, or put a person in front of the outbound step.
All three are present, but a person must approve outbound actions. This holds only if approvers read what is being sent.
Two of three. One more capability turns this into a full path for data theft.
At most one of the three is present, so there is no complete path.

title: Tool timeouts and retries
summary: Some tool calls are slow. See how many time out for a given average latency and timeout, and what retries do to total waiting.

verdicts.text: One task in five fails because a call in it timed out. Raise the timeout toward the slow tail, add retries for safe calls, or make the tool faster.
Timeouts are common enough to notice. Retries help only for idempotent calls.
Timeouts are rare.

tries: Set the timeout close to the average latency.

title: Metric cardinality
summary: Every distinct label combination is a new time series. See how one high-cardinality label multiplies series and memory.

nodes.label: Labels
nodes.sub: user ? 'endpoint, code, instance, user' : 'endpoint, code, instance'

verdicts.text: Millions of series. The server runs out of memory or the bill explodes. Never use unbounded values like user ids, request ids or URLs as labels. Put them in logs or traces.
A large number of series. Check which label multiplies them most.
Bounded labels keep the series count under control.

tries: Turn on the user id label.
Raise endpoints and see how each label multiplies.

title: Alert windows and thresholds
summary: An alert averages errors over a window. See whether a spike of a given size and length fires it, and how soon.

verdicts.text: The spike is short or small enough that the window average never reaches the threshold, so users hurt while nobody is told. Shorten the window or add a fast-burn alert.
It fires, but slowly. A shorter window pages sooner and also fires more on small blips.
The alert fires quickly for this spike.

tries: Use a 60 minute window with a 10 minute spike.
Lower the threshold and see the noise trade-off.

title: Head and tail sampling
summary: Keeping every trace is expensive. See how head sampling can throw away the errors you needed, and what tail sampling costs.

inputs.label: Tail sampling: keep all errors and slow traces

vars: tail ? errs + (rps - errs) * head/100 : rps * head/100

nodes.label: Sampler
nodes.sub: tail ? 'decides after the trace ends' : 'decides at the start'

readouts.label: Error traces thrown away per second

verdicts.text: Head sampling decides before it knows which requests fail, so most error traces are discarded. Tail sampling keeps the interesting ones.
Large storage use. Lower the baseline rate for healthy traces.
Errors are kept and storage is bounded.

chart.y: tail ? rps * err/100 + rps * (1 - err/100) * head/100 : rps * head/100
chart.title: Stored traces against sampling rate

title: Log volume and retention cost
summary: Verbose logs add up quickly. See daily volume, stored volume and relative cost for your retention, and what dropping debug lines saves.

inputs.label: Log lines per second per service
Drop debug lines at the collector

readouts.label: Relative cost, searchable storage as 1 and cheap as 0.1

verdicts.text: Most of the bill is debug noise you rarely read. Drop it at the collector and keep it on only while debugging.
Storage is a large share of the cost. Shorten searchable retention and archive the rest.
Volume and retention are in proportion.

title: What few-shot examples cost
summary: Examples travel with every request. See what they add in tokens and money, and how much caching claws back. Use your own prices.

inputs.label: Share of the example tokens served from cache

verdicts.text: Examples are now a real cost line. Use fewer, better examples, shorten them, or cache the stable prefix.
Examples crowd the context. Check that they still help more than they cost.
A small, affordable overhead.

tries: Use 15 long examples at high volume.

chart.y: reqs * k * tok / 1000000 * price * (1 - cached/100 * (1 - disc/100)) * 30
chart.title: Monthly cost against examples

title: Validate, repair and retry
summary: Model output sometimes fails validation. See how retries and repair prompts change the success rate and the average number of calls.

inputs.label: Chance a repair attempt is valid
Retry with the error message and the bad output

verdicts.text: One in twenty items still fails. Add a fallback, such as a human queue or a safe default, so a failure never reaches users as junk.
Mostly fine, with a small tail of failures. Send the error message back with each retry.
Retries with feedback keep failures rare, at the cost of a few extra calls.

tries: Use 70 percent valid with no retries.

title: Prompt regression check
summary: A new prompt fixes some cases and breaks others. See the net change and why overall score hides the damage.

verdicts.text: The new prompt is worse overall.
The score may rise, but the prompt breaks cases that worked. If those matter to users, hold back and fix them first.
Gains outweigh breaks and breaks are within what you accept.

tries: Read the list of broken cases before shipping.

title: Packing the context
summary: Instructions, retrieved passages, history and the answer all share one window. See what gets squeezed out as you add retrieval.
vars: fit ? k : max(0, floor((window - sys - hist - out) / chunk))

nodes.label: Window
nodes.sub: fit ? round(window - need) + " spare" : round(over) + " over"

verdicts.text: Everything does not fit. Something is truncated, and it is often the end of the prompt where the question or instructions sit. Retrieve fewer, better passages and trim history.
Nearly full. One long user message will overflow it.
There is room for the answer.

title: Threads, processes and the GIL
summary: Run many tasks in parallel. See why threads speed up waiting on the network, but not work that burns CPU.

verdicts.text: CPU-bound threads take turns holding the interpreter lock, so extra threads add overhead and no speed. Use processes, or move the hot loop to native code.
More processes than cores adds switching cost. Match the core count.
The workers genuinely run in parallel here.

tries: Make the work network-bound and add threads.

title: Logging and disk space
summary: A chatty log fills a disk faster than people expect. See how log level and rotation decide how long you have.

nodes.label: Disk
nodes.sub: rotate ? 'kept to ' + fmt(kept, 1) + ' GB' : 'full in ' + fmt(days, 1) + ' days'

readouts.label: Days until the disk is full, no rotation

verdicts.text: The disk fills in days and the service falls over when it does, usually on a weekend. Rotate logs, cap size and ship them off the machine.
Even with rotation, a week of logs does not fit. Lower the level or shorten retention.
It works for now. Without rotation it only postpones the failure.
Rotation keeps logs bounded.

tries: Log 20 lines per request with no rotation.

chart.ylabel: Days until the disk is full
chart.title: Time to full disk

title: Read the file or stream it
summary: Loading a whole file into memory fails once the file outgrows free memory. See where reading in chunks keeps you safe.

inputs.label: Read in chunks or line by line

nodes.label: Program
nodes.sub: stream ? 'one chunk at a time' : 'whole file in memory'

verdicts.text: The program asks for more memory than exists and is killed, often hours into a job. Read in chunks or by line and write results as you go.
It fits, but leaves little room, and a slightly bigger file next week will break it.
Memory use is small and does not grow with the file.

tries: Load a 10 GB file with 4 GB free.

title: Test order and feedback time
summary: A suite has fast and slow tests. See how long you wait to learn about a bug depending on where it is caught and how tests are ordered.
vars: fast ? (where=="u" ? tu : (where=="i" ? tu + ti : all)) : all

readouts.label: Time until you see the failure

verdicts.text: You wait ten minutes or more to learn about a failure. Run the fast tests first and stop on the first failure.
A couple of minutes of waiting adds up across a team.
Feedback arrives quickly.

tries: Catch the bug in a unit test with fast-first off.

title: Defence in depth
summary: No single control stops every attack. See how stacking independent layers cuts what gets through, and why layers that fail together do not add up.

inputs.label: The layers share one weakness (one misconfiguration breaks them all)

verdicts.text: When layers share one weakness they fall together, so you get only the best layer, not the product. Make layers independent: different teams, mechanisms and failure modes.
Too much gets through. Strengthen the weakest layer.
Independent layers multiply, so a good set leaves very little.

title: Secret rotation effort
summary: Rotating a leaked secret means finding every place it lives. See how scattered copies turn a quick fix into a long one, and how a central store helps.

inputs.label: Places per app that hold a copy
Minutes to change and verify one place
Apps read it from one central store at run time

readouts.label: Copies you are likely to miss

verdicts.text: Hours of work while the old secret still works, and some copies will be missed. Keep one source of truth and read it at run time.
Many copies. Each one is something to find during an incident.
One place to change, and everything picks it up.

tries: Use 40 apps in 5 environments with 3 copies each.

chart.y: central ? mins / 60 : apps * envs * places * mins / 60
chart.title: Rotation time against applications

title: Vulnerability backlog
summary: Findings arrive every month and fixes leave at a fixed pace. See whether the backlog shrinks or grows and how long findings stay open.

inputs.label: Days you promise to fix a critical

nodes.label: Backlog
nodes.sub: round(start) + ' now, ' + round(m12) + ' in a year'

verdicts.text: Findings arrive faster than they are fixed, so the backlog grows without end. Fix more, find less noise, or fix by risk and accept the rest.
The backlog shrinks, but the average item waits longer than your promise.
The team keeps pace with new findings.

title: Ransomware and backup retention
summary: Attackers often sit inside before they encrypt. See whether any clean backup is left, and how long a restore takes.

inputs.label: Days the attacker was inside before the attack

readouts.label: Backups that may carry the attacker

verdicts.text: The attacker was inside longer than you keep backups, so every backup may be tainted. Keep older backups and make some immutable.
A clean copy exists, but restoring takes days. Plan what runs in the meantime.
Untested restores usually take longer than the plan says. Test them.
A clean copy exists and the restore is quick enough.

tries: Keep 14 days with a 30 day dwell.

title: Drift and plan frequency
summary: People change things by hand. See how many drifted resources sit unnoticed between plans, and what the next apply will undo.

readouts.label: Average age of a drifted change

verdicts.text: Many resources differ from code by the time you plan. An apply now silently reverts someone urgent fix. Plan on a schedule and alert on drift.
A noticeable amount of drift. Tighten how often you plan.
Frequent plans catch drift while it is small.

tries: Plan every 90 days with 8 hand changes a week.
Reduce hand changes with access controls.

title: count and for_each
summary: Remove one item from a list. With count, everything after it shifts and is replaced. With for_each, only that item goes.

verdicts.text: Count identifies resources by position, so removing one early shifts all the others and Terraform replaces them. For databases or load balancers that means downtime. Use for_each with stable keys.
More than the one you meant is affected.
Only the removed item changes.

tries: Remove the last item with count.

title: Plan time and state size
summary: Every plan refreshes every resource. See how plan time grows with state size, and what splitting states does.

verdicts.text: Plans take ten minutes or more, so people skip them or run them rarely. Split state by lifecycle and ownership, and target what changed.
Slow enough to hurt. A split along team lines helps.
Plans stay quick.

title: Secrets inside state
summary: Marking a value sensitive hides it from output, not from state. See who can read secrets and what protects them.

inputs.label: People with access to the state
Secrets are fetched at run time and not stored in state

vars: sens ? "hidden in plan output" : "printed in plan output"

verdicts.text: Plaintext secrets sit in a state file many people can read. Encrypt the backend, restrict access to a few, and avoid storing secrets in state at all.
Secrets also print in plan output and CI logs. Mark them sensitive, knowing that this hides display only.
Controls limit who can read the state, but the secrets are still in there. Prefer fetching them at run time.
No secrets live in state.

tries: Store 12 secrets with no encryption and 25 readers.
